title: Define a Small Software Problem
why: A small, testable problem gives you a clear way to judge whether the software works.
activity: Choose a recurring task. Write its inputs, outputs, constraints, and three acceptance examples before picking a solution.
evidence: A scoped problem brief and three acceptance examples.
reflection: Which constraint most affected the scope you chose?

title: Implement the Core Logic
why: Boundary cases expose mistakes that a successful demo can hide.
activity: Build the smallest working solution. Compare a straightforward algorithm with an alternative and test empty, typical, and boundary inputs.
evidence: Runnable source, edge-case tests, and a complexity comparison.
reflection: Which input broke your first solution, and why?

title: Design Clear Boundaries
why: Explicit boundaries let you change one concern without rewriting the whole program.
activity: Split input/output concerns from domain logic. Draw module dependencies and record one alternative you rejected.
evidence: A module diagram and architecture decision with rationale.
reflection: Which dependency would make the next change hardest?

title: Connect a Data Source
why: Data contracts fail in ways your core logic must be prepared to handle.
activity: Use a local dataset or documented API. Define a data contract, validate inputs, and handle unavailable or malformed data. Keep fixtures for offline testing.
evidence: A data adapter, local fixture, and failure-handling examples.
reflection: What happens when your data source returns an unexpected value?

title: Debug and Protect Behavior
why: A regression test records why a bug must not return.
activity: Reproduce a defect in your program, locate its cause, and add a meaningful regression test. Run both success and failure cases.
evidence: Reproduction steps, root-cause notes, and passing regression tests.
reflection: Does your test fail before the fix and pass after it?

title: Review a Focused Change
why: A reviewable change lets others understand both the code and your reasoning.
activity: Create a small branch and reviewable change. Ask a peer for feedback, or perform a documented checklist review if a peer is unavailable. Record which type of review happened.
evidence: A focused diff, review notes, and your response to feedback.
reflection: Which feedback changed your implementation or explanation?

title: Improve Maintainability
why: Maintainability matters when someone has to revisit unfamiliar code.
activity: Refactor one confusing module while preserving behavior. Document setup, public contracts, known limits, and test commands.
evidence: Before/after diff, passing checks, and a reproducible README.
reflection: Could someone else run and change the module using only your guide?

title: Prepare a Reproducible Release
why: A release is useful only if others can reproduce it and recover from failure.
activity: Create a versioned build or package. Run release checks in a clean environment and document configuration and recovery steps.
evidence: A versioned artifact, release checklist, and recovery instructions.
reflection: Which release or recovery step was not reproducible at first?

title: Validate With a User
why: Real use challenges assumptions that code tests cannot fully cover.
activity: Ask someone to try the release against the acceptance examples. With consent, record non-identifying feedback and fix one observed issue.
evidence: Anonymized feedback, a follow-up change, and validation results.
reflection: What did the user do differently from your acceptance examples?

title: Publish a Software Case Study
why: A case study makes decisions and their evidence easier to evaluate.
activity: Explain the problem, architecture, algorithm and data decisions, tests, delivery, and limitations. Link reproducible artifacts and distinguish measured results from assumptions.
evidence: A reviewable case study with source, tests, release evidence, and reflection.
reflection: Which outcome can you demonstrate, and which remains an assumption?
